Worth drawing the arrow on the board. Simulation runs the model forwards;

The reason simulation came first: you cannot judge an estimate without knowing
what the truth was, and simulation is the only place you know.
:::

## Why bother estimating parameters?

Because the parameter **is** the biological question:

- **A slope:** how fast is this population declining?
- **A mean:** how many fish does a protected reef hold?
- **A spread:** how variable is egg size between species?
- **A probability:** what fraction of sites are occupied?

. . .

A plot shows you the pattern. A parameter lets you **put a number on it, with
uncertainty**, and compare it to another number.

::: {.notes}
All four examples are from datasets they have handled this semester, which is
deliberate: estimation is not a new activity, it is the thing they have been
circling.

Uncertainty is Thursday's lecture, confidence intervals, and it is the reason
estimation beats eyeballing.
:::

## What is likelihood? {.center}

## The probability of your data

**Likelihood** = the probability of getting the data you actually got, if a
particular set of parameters were true.

. . .

Change the parameters, and that probability changes.

**The maximum likelihood estimate is the parameter value that makes your data
least surprising.**

::: {.notes}
Say the definition slowly, and note the direction: the data are fixed, because
you already collected them, and the parameters are what vary.

That is the opposite of a probability calculation, where the parameters are
fixed and the data vary. Same formula read in the other direction, which is why
it gets a different name.

The last sentence is the one to repeat. Among all the values the parameter could
take, the MLE is the one under which your data look most ordinary.

The figure is the definition made visible. Both panels show what results the
model expects; the only thing that changes is p. Our actual result, 52, sits far
out in the tail when p = 0.5 and right at the peak when p = 0.732. The height of
the red bar is the likelihood, and maximizing it means sliding p until that bar
is as tall as it can be.

The data never move. Only the model does. That is the sentence students need.
:::

## The same data, two models {.smaller}

**The data:** 71 bird survey routes were run in Florida in 2019. Bobwhite were
recorded on **52** of them.

**A model:** every route has the same probability $p$ of holding bobwhite. Below,
what that model expects, for two guesses at $p$.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 2.3
#| fig-width: 9
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(3.2, 3.2, 1.8, 0.6), mgp = c(1.9, 0.6, 0))
kk <- 0:71; obs <- 52
for (pp in c(0.5, 0.732)) {
  d <- dbinom(kk, 71, pp)
  plot(kk, d, type = "h", lwd = 2, col = "grey80",
       xlab = "routes with bobwhite, out of 71",
       ylab = "P(exactly this many)", ylim = c(0, 0.13),
       main = paste0("if p = ", pp))
  lines(c(obs, obs), c(0, d[kk == obs]), col = "firebrick", lwd = 3)
  points(obs, d[kk == obs], pch = 16, col = "firebrick", cex = 1.2)
  lab <- if (d[kk == obs] < 0.001) format(d[kk == obs], digits = 2,
                                          scientific = TRUE) else
         sprintf("%.3f", d[kk == obs])
  text(obs, d[kk == obs] + 0.015, lab, col = "firebrick", font = 2)
}
```


Each grey bar is the probability of **one possible result**, 0 to 71 routes; they
add to 1. Red is the result **we got**.

**That red height is the likelihood:** 0.00004 on the left, 0.106 on the right.

::: {.notes}
The definition made visible. Both panels show what results the model expects, and
the only thing that changes between them is p.

Be explicit about what the y axis is, because this is the slide where people
quietly substitute a p-value. Each bar is the probability of exactly that many
routes having bobwhite, under the model. Our red bar is the probability of
exactly 52, which is the likelihood.

It is NOT the probability of 52 or more, which is what a p-value would be, and it
is not the probability that p = 0.5 is true. Probability of the data given the
parameter, never the other way round. If someone asks about p-values, say that a
p-value adds up a tail of these bars and answers a different question, and that
we are not doing that today.

The data never move. Only the model does. That is the sentence students need, and
it is the one that makes the next few slides obvious: if the bar gets taller as
you change p, you are going the right way.

Maximizing likelihood means sliding p until that red bar is as tall as it can be,
which is literally what the curve two slides from now shows.
:::

## Refresher: the `d` functions give probabilities {.smaller}

From Lecture 12. Every `d` function takes two things: **the data** and
**the parameters**.

```{r}
dbinom(x = 7, size = 10, prob = 0.5)    # P(7 heads in 10 tosses) if p = 0.5
```

. . .

Which one you hold still decides what you are asking:

```{r}
#| eval: false
dbinom(x = 0:10, size = 10, prob = 0.5)              # parameter fixed, data vary

dbinom(x = 7, size = 10, prob = c(0.3, 0.5, 0.7))    # data fixed, parameter varies
```

. . .

The first asks **what results to expect**. The second asks **which parameter
best accounts for the result I got**. Your data are already collected and will
not change, so the parameter is the thing that moves. That second one is
likelihood.

::: {.notes}
Two minutes, but worth it, because the whole lecture is built on d functions and
some will have met them only once.

Run both lines live if you can. The first returns eleven numbers, one per
possible result, and they add to 1: that is a probability distribution. The
second returns three numbers, one per candidate value of p, and they do not add
to anything in particular: that is a likelihood.

That is the conceptual jump of the chapter, and it is purely about which argument
you let vary. Same function, same arithmetic, different question.

The sentence worth repeating: the data are fixed because you already went out and
collected them. The parameter is unknown, so it is the thing you move.
:::

## A question with one parameter

Of **71** Florida routes surveyed in 2019, bobwhite were recorded on **52**.

. . .

If each route has the same probability $p$ of holding bobwhite, **what is $p$?**

. . .

You already know the answer is 52/71. Good: that means you can check whether
likelihood gives the right answer on a problem where you can see it.

::: {.notes}
Deliberately a problem where the answer is obvious, because the point is to
validate the machinery rather than to learn the answer.

The model: each route is a coin flip with probability p, and 52 of 71 came up
heads. That is a binomial.

Independence between routes is an assumption and it is worth naming out loud,
because routes near each other share habitat.
:::

## Try one value {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

If $p$ were 0.5, how likely is 52 out of 71?

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
dbinom(x = 52, size = 71, prob = 0.5)
```
:::

. . .

Now try `prob = 0.6`, then `0.73`, then `0.8`. Which gives the biggest number?

::: {.notes}
Three minutes, and this is the whole idea in one line of code.

The numbers: 0.0000367 at p = 0.5, 0.0069 at 0.6, 0.106 at 0.73, 0.0415 at 0.8.

Two things to draw out. The likelihood at p = 0.5 is tiny, because 52 of 71 would
be a strange result if routes were coin flips. And the value peaks somewhere near
0.73, which they can find by hand before any optimizer appears.
:::

## Try every value

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 3.1
#| fig-width: 7
p_grid <- seq(0.4, 1, by = 0.001)
L <- dbinom(with_bobwhite, routes_2019, p_grid)
plot(p_grid, L, type = "l", lwd = 3, xlab = "p", ylab = "likelihood of our data")
abline(v = with_bobwhite / routes_2019, col = "red", lwd = 2, lty = 2)
text(with_bobwhite / routes_2019, max(L) * 0.55,
     paste0(" 52/71 = ", round(with_bobwhite / routes_2019, 3)), col = "red", adj = 0)
```

The curve peaks exactly at **52/71 = 0.732**. The machinery agrees with the
obvious answer.

::: {.notes}
This is the likelihood curve, and it is the central picture of the chapter.

Two features worth naming: the peak is the estimate, and the width is the
uncertainty. A sharp peak means the data pin the parameter down; a flat one means
many values explain the data about equally well. Thursday turns that width into
a confidence interval.

For a binomial the MLE is provably the sample proportion. Most problems have no
such formula, which is why the next few slides reach for an optimizer.
:::

## What if you have more than one observation? {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

So far, one number: 52 out of 71. The bobwhite **counts** are 1360 numbers.

If the observations are independent, the probability of getting **all** of them
is each probability **multiplied together**:

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
dpois(bobwhite[1:5], lambda = 10.8)        # probability of each of the first 5

prod(dpois(bobwhite[1:5], lambda = 10.8))  # all five together

prod(dpois(bobwhite[1:50], lambda = 10.8)) # fifty

prod(dpois(bobwhite, lambda = 10.8))       # all 1360
```
:::

**What happened on that last line?**

::: {.notes}
Five minutes, and the punchline has to be discovered rather than announced.

The numbers: five counts multiply to 2.4e-23, fifty to 1.9e-303, and all 1360 to
exactly 0. R cannot hold anything smaller than about 2.2e-308, so the answer is
not merely small, it is gone.

That is a disaster for an optimizer: every parameter value returns zero, so there
is nothing to climb. The fix is the next slide.

Poisson is a stand-in here, purely to have something to multiply. The right
distribution for these counts is the one we settled on Thursday, and it comes
back shortly.
:::

## Why we use logs {.smaller}

You just watched the product of 1360 probabilities collapse to zero:

$$L = \prod_i P(y_i \mid \text{parameters})$$

. . .

Nothing is wrong with the arithmetic. The number really is that small, and the
computer cannot hold it. Taking logs turns multiplication into addition:

$$\log L = \sum_i \log P(y_i \mid \text{parameters})$$

. . .

By convention we minimize the **negative** log-likelihood, because optimizers
minimize.

::: {.notes}
Three reasons for logs, in order of importance: products of thousands of small
numbers underflow to zero in floating point, as they just saw, sums are easier to
differentiate,
and the log scale makes the surface better behaved for optimizers.

The negative is pure convention: R's optimizers minimize, so we hand them the
negative and the minimum of the negative is the maximum of the original.

Point at the product and the sum: that is why every d function has a log = TRUE
argument, which is the next slide.
:::

## Why the optimizer prefers the log {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 2.9
#| fig-width: 9
set.seed(5)
sub <- sample(bobwhite, 50)
m <- mean(sub)
lam <- seq(max(0.5, m - 8), m + 8, by = 0.05)
lik <- sapply(lam, function(l) prod(dpois(sub, l)))
llik <- sapply(lam, function(l) sum(dpois(sub, l, log = TRUE)))
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(3.4, 4.4, 2.0, 0.6), mgp = c(2.6, 0.6, 0))
plot(lam, lik, type = "l", lwd = 3, xlab = "lambda", ylab = "likelihood",
     main = "likelihood (50 counts)")
abline(v = m, col = "red", lty = 2, lwd = 2)
plot(lam, llik, type = "l", lwd = 3, xlab = "lambda", ylab = "log-likelihood",
     main = "log-likelihood (same 50 counts)")
abline(v = m, col = "red", lty = 2, lwd = 2)
```

Same data, same peak (red). On the left the curve is flat at zero almost
everywhere; on the right there is a slope to follow from anywhere.

::: {.notes}
This is the practical argument, and it is worth more than the underflow one.

An optimizer works by looking at where it is, asking which way is uphill, and
stepping. On the left, the whole curve lives between 0 and 7e-168, so outside a
window of about two either side of the peak it is indistinguishable from flat:
there is nothing to tell the optimizer which way to go.

On the right the log-likelihood has a clear slope everywhere, so a starting guess
of 4 or 20 still finds its way to the top.

Only 50 counts are used here, so that the likelihood is at least representable.
With all 1360 the left panel would be exactly zero across the whole range and
there would be nothing to plot at all.

The peak is in the same place in both, which is the mathematical point: the log
is a monotonic transformation, so whatever maximizes the likelihood maximizes its
log. We change the scale, not the answer.
:::

## A refresher on writing functions {.smaller}

From Lecture 9: name, arguments, body, and the last line is the result.

```{r}
#| eval: false
standard_error <- function(x){
  sd(x) / sqrt(length(x))
}
```

. . .

To use an optimizer, you hand it a function to minimize. So we write one that
takes a parameter and returns a negative log-likelihood:

```{r}
#| eval: false
nll_name <- function(parameter){
  -sum(dsomething(data, parameter, log = TRUE))
}
```

::: {.notes}
Deliberately brief, because they wrote several functions in Lecture 9 and a few
since.

The shape of an NLL function is worth naming as a pattern, because every one they
write for the rest of the course looks like this: parameters in, a single number
out, and a minus sign at the front.
:::

## The negative log-likelihood, for real {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
binom_nll <- function(p){
  -dbinom(x = with_bobwhite, size = routes_2019, prob = p, log = TRUE)
}

binom_nll(0.5)
binom_nll(0.732)
```
:::

Smaller is better: the second is the one that makes our data less surprising.

::: {.notes}
Five minutes. Note there is no sum here because there is a single observation,
52 out of 71. The sum appears in the next example.

10.21 against 2.24. Worth connecting back: those are the logs of the 0.0000367
and 0.106 from earlier, negated.
:::

## Let R find the minimum {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
fit <- optimize(binom_nll, interval = c(0, 1))

fit$minimum       # the estimate
fit$objective     # the negative log-likelihood there
```
:::

. . .

`optimize()` for one parameter, `optim()` for several.

::: {.notes}
0.7324 and 2.236. Compare to 52/71 = 0.73239, which is what the formula gives.

Say what the optimizer actually does: it tries values, climbs downhill, and stops
when it cannot improve. It is a careful version of what they did by hand three
slides ago, and like anything numerical it can fail, which is why a plot of the
curve is still worth drawing.
:::

## Two parameters: back to the counts {.center}

## Thursday's unfinished business {.smaller}

On Thursday we needed a negative binomial for the bobwhite counts, and got its
clumping parameter by **matching the variance**:

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
mu_moment <- mean(bobwhite)
size_moment <- mu_moment^2 / (var(bobwhite) - mu_moment)

round(c(mu = mu_moment, size = size_moment), 3)
```
:::

That was a shortcut. **Maximum likelihood is the principled version**, and it
uses the whole distribution rather than two summaries.

::: {.notes}
The thread from Thursday, picked up deliberately: the moment estimate was
introduced as a stopgap with a promise that chapter 6 would do it properly.

Method of moments matches the mean and the variance and ignores everything else
about the shape. Likelihood asks which parameters make every observed count, all
1360 of them, most probable together.

They should expect the two answers to be close but not identical, and they are
about to see exactly that.
:::

## The likelihood surface {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 3.3
#| fig-width: 6.6
mus <- seq(9.5, 12.5, length.out = 80)
sizes <- seq(0.9, 2.0, length.out = 80)
grid <- outer(mus, sizes, Vectorize(function(m, s)
  -sum(dnbinom(bobwhite, mu = m, size = s, log = TRUE))))
contour(mus, sizes, grid, nlevels = 25, xlab = "mu", ylab = "size (clumping)",
        drawlabels = FALSE, col = "grey55")
best <- which(grid == min(grid), arr.ind = TRUE)
points(mus[best[1]], sizes[best[2]], pch = 16, col = "red", cex = 1.6)
points(mu_moment, size_moment, pch = 17, col = "blue", cex = 1.4)
legend("topright", pch = c(16, 17), col = c("red", "blue"), bty = "n",
       legend = c("maximum likelihood", "method of moments"))
```

With two parameters the likelihood is a **surface**, and the estimate is its
lowest point on the negative log scale.

::: {.notes}
The contour lines are negative log-likelihood, so the target is the bottom of the
bowl rather than the top of a hill.

Point at the shape. The contours are closed ellipses with their axes roughly
lined up with the parameter axes, which means the two parameters are nearly
independent here: knowing the mean better would not tell you much more about the
clumping.

How tightly each is pinned down comes from the curvature, and with 1360
observations both are tight: the mean is 10.79 give or take 0.27, the clumping
1.37 give or take 0.06. Beware reading that off the picture by eye, because the
two axes are on different scales. Turning curvature into an interval properly is
Thursday.

The two markers are close but not on top of each other, which is the point of the
next slide.
:::

## Fitting it {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
nb_nll <- function(mu, size){
  -sum(dnbinom(bobwhite, mu = mu, size = size, log = TRUE))
}

fit_nb <- optim(par = c(mu = 10, size = 1),
                fn = function(p){
                  nb_nll(p["mu"], p["size"])
                },
                method = "BFGS")

round(fit_nb$par, 3)
```
:::

| | mu | size |
|---|---|---|
| method of moments | 10.78 | **1.155** |
| maximum likelihood | 10.79 | **1.368** |

::: {.notes}
Eight minutes, and the first time they fit a two-parameter model to real data.

The means agree to two decimals. The clumping does not, by about 18%, and
likelihood is the one to trust: moments threw away everything except the mean and
the variance, and with a long-tailed distribution that is a lot to discard.

Which matters practically: size is what drove the power analysis on Thursday, so
the choice of estimator changes the study design advice.

If optim complains or returns something absurd, check the starting values. Four
things to know about optimizers: they need a starting point, they can fail, they
report whether they converged, and a plot is the sanity check.
:::

## The same fit, with `mle2` {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

Bolker's package wraps the same idea in a friendlier interface. **Do the two
routes agree?**

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
library(bbmle)

m1 <- mle2(minuslogl = nb_nll,
           start = list(mu = 10, size = 1),
           data = list(bobwhite = bobwhite))

coef(m1)

coef(m1) - fit_nb$par        # should be about zero
```
:::

::: {.notes}
Five minutes. The differences come out as zeros, which is the right answer and
also worth being honest about: mle2 calls optim underneath, so with the same
starting values it walks the same path. This checks that we wired both up
correctly, not that two independent algorithms agree.

The stronger version of the check, if anyone wants it: add method = "Nelder-Mead"
to one of them and compare again. A different search algorithm landing in the
same place is real reassurance.

Why check at all: an optimizer is a numerical search, not a formula. It can stop
early, stop in the wrong place, or fail silently, so comparing routes and looking
at the curve are both cheap insurance. That habit matters more in the final
project than anything else on this slide.

Chapter 6 uses mle2 throughout, and it has confidence interval methods built in,
which is Thursday. optim is the thing to understand; mle2 is the convenience.
:::

## Remember why we rejected the Poisson {.smaller}

On Thursday we tested it against these same counts:

| | observed | Poisson said |
|---|---|---|
| variance | 111 | 11 |
| P(count $\geq$ 40) | 0.024 | 0.000000000007 |

We threw it out on those two rows. **Likelihood lets us put one number on how
much worse it was.**

::: {.notes}
The reminder matters, because the next slide compares two models and nobody will
remember why a Poisson is even in the conversation.

Thursday's argument was a model check: the Poisson predicts a variance equal to
its mean, and these counts have a variance ten times their mean, so it cannot
reproduce the spread or the occasional very rich route.

That was a yes-or-no verdict. Likelihood turns it into a measurement, which is
what the next slide does and what next week builds on.
:::

## Was the negative binomial worth it? {.smaller}

A Poisson has one parameter, and its best value is just the mean, so there is
nothing to optimize:

```{r}
nll_poisson <- -sum(dpois(bobwhite, lambda = mean(bobwhite), log = TRUE))
nll_negbin <- fit_nb$value

round(c(poisson = nll_poisson, negative_binomial = nll_negbin))
```

The negative binomial is **thousands** of log-likelihood units better.

. . .

How much better is "better enough"? **That is next week.**

::: {.notes}
8455 against 4627. Not a close call, which is the right first example of a model
comparison: when the answer is this obvious you do not need a test.

The honest complication, which is next week's lecture: the negative binomial has
an extra parameter, so it has an unfair advantage, and model comparison is about
paying for that advantage. Name the problem and leave it.
:::

## Your turn: estimate the decline {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

Thursday we **assumed** a 3% decline. Now estimate it from the counts:

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
bob <- bbs[bbs$Scientific_Name == "Colinus virginianus", ]
counts <- bob$total_sightings
year <- bob$Year - min(bob$Year)        # 0, 1, 2, ... 23

trend_nll <- function(mu0, decline, size){
  mu <- mu0 * (1 - decline)^year        # the mean declines each year
  # your negative log-likelihood goes here
  # (hint: you wrote one for these counts a few slides ago)
}

fit_trend <- optim(par = c(mu0 = 15, decline = 0.03, size = 1),
                   fn = function(p){
                     # call your NLL function here, with the three parameters
                   },
                   method = "L-BFGS-B",
                   lower = c(0.1, -0.5, 0.05),
                   upper = c(100, 0.5, 50))

fit_trend$par
```
:::

**What annual decline did you get? Compare it to the 3% we assumed.**

::: {.notes}
Ten minutes, and it is the capstone: the model they simulated from on Thursday,
now fitted to the real counts.

Two things to supply, and both are recall rather than fill-in-the-blank. The body
of trend_nll is one line, the same shape as the nb_nll they wrote earlier:
-sum(dnbinom(counts, mu = mu, size = size, log = TRUE)). The optim wrapper is
trend_nll(p["mu0"], p["decline"], p["size"]).

Point anyone who is stuck back at the "Fitting it" slide rather than telling
them. The two pieces are the same pattern with one extra parameter.

The answer: mu0 about 14.8 birds per route in 1996, decline 0.0291, so 2.9% a
year, and size 1.43. The 3% we assumed on Thursday came from a published trend,
and the data agree with it to within a tenth of a percent, which is a satisfying
place to end.

Why L-BFGS-B and bounds rather than BFGS: without bounds the optimizer wanders
into negative sizes and declines above 1, which produce NaNs and a screenful of
warnings. Bounds keep it in the region where the model means something. Worth
naming as a general habit for constrained parameters.

For anyone who asks whether the trend is "significant": the no-trend fit had an
NLL of 4627 and this one has 4596, so the trend buys about 31 units. Whether that
is enough, given it costs a parameter, is exactly next week.
:::

## Your turn: a different species {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
# pick a species, any species

counts <- bbs$total_sightings[bbs$Scientific_Name == "____"]

mean(counts)
var(counts) / mean(counts)        # still clumped?

nb_nll2 <- function(mu, size){
  -sum(dnbinom(counts, mu = mu, size = size, log = TRUE))
}

optim(par = c(mu = mean(counts), size = 1),
      fn = function(p){

        # call your NLL function here, with the two parameters

      },
      method = "BFGS")$par
```
:::

How does the fitted `size` compare with the moment estimate,
`mean(counts)^2 / (var(counts) - mean(counts))`?

::: {.notes}
If there is time, or as practice afterwards. Letting them choose means the room
produces a dozen different answers, which is better than everyone checking the
same number.

Finding the species names is part of the exercise: the column is
bbs$Scientific_Name, and table() or unique() on it will do. They have both.

The starting value for mu comes from the data rather than a fixed number, so the
code works whichever species they pick. Worth pointing out: a sensible starting
guess is the difference between an optimizer that converges and one that does
not.

What they will find, from a few I ran:

- Northern Cardinal: mu 51.2, size 1.95 by moments, 2.55 by likelihood
- Northern Mockingbird: mu 33.2, size 1.34 by moments, 1.18 by likelihood
- Common Grackle: mu 22.3, size 0.59 by moments, 0.85 by likelihood

So the two estimators disagree, sometimes in one direction and sometimes the
other. Do not promise them a pattern. The point is that moments and likelihood
are answering slightly different questions, and likelihood is the one with the
better justification.

Anyone who finishes early: try a species with few records, such as Florida
Scrub-Jay with about 100, and watch the estimate wobble. That is the small-sample
problem confidence intervals exist for, which is Thursday.
:::

## What you can now do

- Write down the probability of your data under a model
- Turn it into a negative log-likelihood
- Hand that to an optimizer and get **estimates from real data**

. . .

Still missing: **how sure are you?** That is Thursday.

::: {.notes}
Worth saying that this is the moment the course turns from describing to
inferring, and that everything after it is refinement.
:::
